The question of whether birds descend from dinosaurs is the subject of genuine scientific debate, with a strong mainstream consensus and a notable minority dissent. The dominant scientific view, supported by multiple high-credibility sources, holds that birds are the only living descendants of dinosaurs, specifically having evolved from theropod dinosaurs including bipedal carnivores such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor [d6][d2][d5]. Fossils have confirmed to "all but a few skeptics" that birds descended from dinosaurs and are living representatives of the Maniraptoran lineage [d5], and coelurosaurian dinosaurs are considered the closest relatives of birds [d3].

However, a minority of researchers actively contest this view. An alternate theory, espoused by scientists such as Larry Martin and Alan Feduccia, holds that birds evolved from early archosaurs like Longisquama rather than from dinosaurs, though this is contested by most paleontologists [d7]. A 2010 study published in PNAS provided evidence that birds did not descend from ground-dwelling theropod dinosaurs, with zoologist John Ruben suggesting that some species believed to be dinosaurs may have actually descended from birds [d8]. Similarly, fossil finds from the Middle Jurassic of China have been cited by some researchers as evidence that birds evolved from a separate lineage of non-dinosaurian archosaurs, not the lineage leading to theropods [d1]. Despite these challenges, the University of California Museum of Paleontology notes that the evidence for the dinosaurian origin theory has so far "swamped" the efforts of those trying to falsify it [d3].
